objects.name: Crowd Out Contributions to an Information Space
objects.description:
Summary:
Crowd Out Contributions to an Information Space describes the deliberate saturation of a specific, bounded space with content, so that it can no longer effectively carry the information it otherwise would. It is not the same as producing a large volume of content; an actor is only crowding out contributions if a particular information space was saturated.

Detail:
For the purposes of this Technique, an information space is defined as any information ecosystem where an individual could reasonably expect to access a collection of information on a given topic, theme, or collection of topics. Public information spaces include the material carried alongside a hashtag, the comments on a post or article, the chat accompanying a live stream, and a user's feed or timeline. Private information spaces include a group chat, a person's direct messages, and an email inbox. Identifying the affected space is therefore a precondition for identifying this Technique; an actor producing a large volume of content is not crowding out contributions unless the analyst can name the space that content has saturated.

Contributions to an information space are crowded out when the space receives an influx of content exceeding the levels of activity typical for that space, displacing the content it would otherwise carry. A space's average activity changes what qualifies; a group chat could be saturated by 100 messages, where the same activity wouldn't register as abnormal on a busy hashtag. However, crowding out requires a plurality of content. A single contribution which renders a space unusable is disruption of a different kind.

Where a space has an observable history, crowding out can be identified by comparing activity against average metrics for a comparable timeframe. Where a space has no history, either because it is private or because the space was created by the activity itself, as when an actor occupies a hashtag previously unused, the comparison is against what the space would reasonably be expected to carry rather than against a measured baseline.

An information space being saturated is not by itself an indicator of malicious behaviour. There can be a naturally occurring spike in activity in response to events, such as a mass of anguished posting after conceding a goal in the final minutes of a World Cup match. This surge of posts can have the impact of making it harder to find any other topic on one's timeline. What makes crowding out a Technique is that the volume of content is the intention of the behaviour, rather than emerging from organic activity. In an organic surge, individual participants post for their own reasons and the aggregate effect is a byproduct of many independent decisions; in crowding out, an actor posts in order to occupy a space, whether by coordinating many assets posting in near-simultaneity or by repeatedly publishing from a single asset.

Because volume is the important element of crowding out, actors don't need to curate a persona or craft a narrative to achieve their effect. Content used to crowd out contributions is frequently duplicated or near-duplicated; [research on political WhatsApp groups in Brazil](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/31354) characterises what its authors call flooding attacks as the sharing of large numbers of usually duplicate messages within a short window. Content is also frequently irrelevant to the space it occupies, since relevance is not required for displacement; in the WhatsApp study, 62% of these attacks were carried out using stickers, content carrying almost no semantic payload. Where the objective is to alter the meaning of a space rather than merely obstruct it, content is instead matched to the target, as in [the saturation of the #DoctorsSpeakUp vaccination campaign hashtag with anti-vaccine material](https://www.newsweek.com/doctors-speak-twitter-trend-anti-vaxxers-vaccine-hashtag-1490692).

Crowding Out Contributions as a Method of Information Suppression:
[A study of 19 million messages across roughly 1,600 Brazilian public political WhatsApp groups](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/31354) identified these attacks in approximately 7% of groups, defined as an attacker sharing a large number of usually duplicate messages within a short period, with most attacks resolving in under four minutes. This qualifies as crowding out contributions to an information space; the space is tightly bounded, being a single group with a small membership and a linear message feed, so its carrying capacity is low and easily exceeded. The volume is intended rather than organically occurring, since the messages are duplicates published by an attacker rather than independent contributions by members. And the content was not the payload: 62% of the attacks were carried out using stickers, which convey almost nothing. Nobody was being argued with; their information space was being attacked. The suppressive effect follows from the mechanism rather than from any message. Nothing was deleted, no member was removed, and the group continued to exist; what stopped was the group's usability. Members could not follow a conversation, locate earlier messages, or coordinate, because the feed had been consumed.

Crowding out can suppress without the displacing content being noise. In March 2020 the physician Zubin Damania launched #DoctorsSpeakUp to coordinate doctors posting publicly in support of vaccination. Anti-vaccine accounts adopted the hashtag in volume, and research found that [the majority of tweets carrying it were oriented against vaccines](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10410236.2022.2058159), with fewer than 17% coming from pro-vaccine doctors who identified themselves as such. The mechanism is the same as in the WhatsApp groups: intended volume into a bounded space, exceeding what that space would ordinarily carry. What differs is the composition of the displacing content, and therefore what followed. While the WhatsApp groups lost functionality as an information space, the hashtag kept functioning, but the message associated with it had been reversed. The pro-vaccine doctors were not only displaced from the space they had created; the space now argued against them.

Crowding out is not limited to spaces where people talk to each other. The US Federal Communications Commission's 2017 public consultation on repealing net neutrality received roughly 22 million comments, orders of magnitude above what such a consultation ordinarily receives. [An investigation found that around 18 million of them were fraudulent](https://ag.ny.gov/sites/default/files/reports/oag-fakecommentsreport.pdf), including 8.5 million opposing net neutrality submitted through a $4.2 million campaign funded by the broadband industry, which used the identities of real people without their consent. The fraud was not one-sided; the same investigation found that a single 19-year-old submitted over 7.7 million pro-net-neutrality comments using fabricated identities. The consultation record is a bounded information space; it is the permanent, publicly accessible collection of responses to a defined question, relied on by the agency at the time and by any court reviewing the decision afterwards. As with the hashtag, it continued to function; what it stopped doing was carrying the views of the people who had genuinely submitted them, which survived only as a small minority of a record overwhelmingly composed of fabrications, while some real people found their names attached to positions they had never held. The case also demonstrates that this Technique does not require a network of collaborating individuals, since 7.7 million of those submissions came from one person.

Crowding Out Contributions as a Method of Harassment:
Twitch hate raids are an example of deploying Crowd Out Contributions to an Information Space as a form of harassment. From mid-2021, automated accounts filled individual streamers' live chats with racist, misogynist, and antisemitic content while they were broadcasting. Twitch [sued two users](https://techcrunch.com/2021/09/13/twitch-hate-raids-lawsuits/) in September 2021, alleging that one of them alone was linked to around 3,000 bot accounts, and the practice has since been studied in two CSCW papers ([Cai et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.16248); [Han et al., 2023](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.03946)). The space is a single channel's live chat, which is easily saturated since it is an unthreaded scrolling window displaying ten to twenty messages with no search and no persistence. Displacement is therefore total and immediate at volumes that would have less impact in other information spaces.

The harassment element is compounded by the volume of abuse. The target cannot moderate at the rate of arrival, so the ordinary defensive tools, if any are available, fail as a countermeasure. The target's own community is displaced along with the abuse, so the harm is not only to the individual but to the space they built and the relationships in it. And the abuse is public and synchronous, witnessed live by whoever remained, which exacerbates the reputational and emotional dimensions. The same dynamic appears in individual rather than broadcast spaces, as when [Maria Ressa reported receiving an average of 90 hate messages per hour](https://gijn.org/stories/online-harassment-lessons-from-the-philippines/) for a month after Rappler published its investigation into networked political trolling in the Philippines.

Contributions Crowded Out Organically:
On 2 June 2020, during the protests following the killing of George Floyd, millions of users posted plain black squares to Instagram as part of Blackout Tuesday, an initiative conceived by the music industry figures Jamila Thomas and Brianna Agyemang. A large proportion tagged those posts #BlackLivesMatter and #BLM, and the tags were saturated within hours. The material displaced was operational: protest logistics, safety guidance, bail fund details, contacts for lawyers offering pro bono representation, and video documentation of police conduct. [Organisers publicly asked participants to strip the BLM tags from their posts and to use #BlackoutTuesday or #TheShowMustBePaused instead](https://time.com/5846514/blackout-tuesday-screen/). On every observable measure contributions to this information space were crowded out: the space was bounded, the volume vastly exceeded anything the tag would ordinarily carry, and content that people had a reasonable expectation of finding there became unreachable at the moment it was most needed.

This example demonstrates that the impact of behaviour is not what defines Technique usage. The volume was emergent rather than intended. Each participant posted once, sincerely, in support of the movement whose information they buried, and nobody was acting in order to occupy the space. The correction is itself evidence of this; participants removed the tags once the effect was explained to them, and an actor crowding out contributions deliberately does not stop on being told that it is working.

Differentiating Crowding Out Contributions from Astroturfing:
Crowding out and astroturfing are often conflated, but they are separated by what the volume of messaging is for. [Astroturfing is conventionally defined](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10584609.2019.1661888) as a centrally coordinated campaign in which participants pretend to be ordinary citizens acting independently, concealing the sponsor so that an orchestrated message appears to be spontaneous public sentiment. In astroturfing, the volume of messaging is evidence to support the claim that many independent people hold this view. In crowding out, the volume of messaging occupies a space, and nothing about it needs to be believed.

One way to differentiate between astroturfing and crowding out is whether public attribution of activity neutralises the behaviour. Astroturfing is less effective once exposed, because credibility of the messaging is important to its success. Contributions to an information space continue to be crowded out after everyone knows what is happening, which is why the [Brazilian political WhatsApp groups](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/31354) remained unusable whether or not their members understood that the stickers were an attack.

A second differentiator is the minimum volume each requires. Astroturfing has no volume floor; a small number of accounts posting considered content while presenting as unconnected individuals is astroturfing and nothing else. Crowding out has a minimum volume, since it is defined by exceeding a space's capacity. Volume is therefore a requirement of crowding out, and merely an element of some astroturfing campaigns.

The behaviours are not mutually exclusive. An incident may be both crowding out and astroturfing. The FCC consultation is the clearest instance in this entry: submitting 8.5 million responses in the names of real people manufactures the appearance of independent public support, which is astroturfing, while 18 million fraudulent submissions overwhelming a 22 million response record is crowding out.
